267.title: Hamzah, lion of Allah
267.hook: his uncle Hamzah, the lion of Allah, is killed at Uhud, and the Prophet ﷺ grieves
267.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Medina visit the graves of Hamzah and the martyrs of Uhud at the foot of the mountain, greeting them and praying for them, and many Muslims name their sons Hamzah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hill at Uhud, and the archers who left too soon. Your line was hold the hill. Did you finish the thing you wanted to leave early? Day two hundred sixty-seven.

Years before Medina, back in Mecca, a big, proud hunter comes home from the desert with his bow on his shoulder. A woman stops him: while you were gone, Abu Jahl insulted your nephew Muhammad to his face, and he said nothing back. The hunter turns around, walks straight into the gathering of Quraysh, finds Abu Jahl, and strikes him with his bow. Then he says, in front of everyone: I follow his religion too. Hit me back if you can. That was Hamzah, uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and from that day, the biographers say, Quraysh thought twice about harming the Prophet. Today, the man they called the lion of God.
screen: `A HUNTER COMES HOME.` → `HE STRIKES ABU JAHL.` → `I FOLLOW HIS RELIGION TOO.`

segments.voice: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was the Prophet's uncle, but the biographers say close to him in age, and the two had been nursed by the same woman as babies. The Prophet called him his brother through nursing. He was strong, fearless, and at Badr he fought at the front. People called him asad Allah, the lion of God. But at Uhud there was a man watching for him. Wahshi was an Abyssinian slave in Mecca, skilled with a short throwing spear. His master had promised him his freedom if he killed Hamzah, whose sword had killed the master's uncle at Badr. Wahshi told the story himself, years later, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. He hid behind a rock, waited for Hamzah to pass, and threw. Hamzah fell. After the battle, his body was found mutilated. The early biographers describe the Prophet standing over him in deep grief. Back in Medina, he heard the women of the Ansar weeping for their dead, and he said: but Hamzah has no women to weep for him. And the women of Medina came to his door to weep for Hamzah. Tradition calls Hamzah the master of the martyrs, and his grave lies at the foot of Uhud. And here is the part that's hardest. Years later, Wahshi became Muslim and came to the Prophet. The Prophet did not turn him away. Bukhari says he asked one question: are you the one who killed Hamzah? Wahshi said it was as he'd been told. And then the Prophet said: can you keep your face out of my sight? He accepted him. He still grieved. Both were true.
screen: `ASAD ALLAH — THE LION OF GOD.` · `WAHSHI BEHIND THE ROCK.` · `NO ONE TO WEEP FOR HAMZAH.` · `ACCEPTED, AND STILL GRIEVED.` · then, large: `THE LION FELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone brave. Sit, and let a person come to mind who stood up when it cost them something. It could be someone famous, or someone only you know: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who spoke up for you in a room where nobody else would. If they've died, let yourself miss them for a minute, the way the Prophet missed Hamzah. If you pray, you can make du'a for them. The bell holds the time.
Hamzah. The Prophet's uncle and nursing brother, the lion of God, killed at Uhud and remembered as the master of the martyrs. Today's word.
Your line: the lion fell. Today, tell someone about the brave person you remembered, so they're honored out loud. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

268.title: The Trench
268.hook: Salman the Persian suggests a trench, and all dig, the Prophet ﷺ among them, hungry (33:9–11)
268.howItsDone: Muslims remember the battle of the Trench through Surah al-Ahzab, and Salman al-Farisi is honored as an example of a seeker from far away, embraced by the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hamzah, the lion of God, and a grief that still made room for his killer. Your line was the lion fell. Did you tell someone about a brave person you remembered? Day two hundred sixty-eight.

After Uhud, the news gets worse. Mecca has gathered allies from across Arabia. The biographers put the army at about ten thousand, coming to finish Medina for good, and the city's fighters at maybe three thousand. There's no wall. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls his companions together to plan, and the ideas go around the circle. And then a man speaks up who isn't from Mecca, or from Medina, or from Arabia at all. He's a Persian, a former slave, and he says: where I come from, when we're besieged, we dig a trench. The early biographers say no one in Arabia had fought that way before. Today: the Trench.

The man was Salman al-Farisi, Salman the Persian. He had left his home in Persia as a young man searching for the truth, traveled through Syria, been sold into slavery, and ended up in Medina, where he became Muslim. The Prophet took his idea, and the Muslims of the city dug. The trench ran across the open northern side of Medina, where horsemen could charge. It was winter, and cold. Food was so short that, Jabir says in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet had a stone bound against his stomach to quiet the hunger. Another report there says he carried earth until the dust covered his belly, and chanted with the diggers as they worked. When they hit a rock no one could break, they called him, and he took the pickaxe himself and struck until it crumbled. Then the army arrived, and stopped. Horses can't jump a deep ditch. The siege dragged on for weeks. The Qur'an describes how it felt inside the city: the enemy came at you from above and below, eyes grew wild, hearts rose into throats, and the believers were shaken hard. And then, it says, God sent a wind, and hosts they could not see. The biographers say a cold, violent wind tore through the enemy camp at night, overturning pots and blowing out fires, and the great army packed up and left. The Muslims remember it as the battle of the Trench, or the Confederates, al-Ahzab, the name of the surah that tells it. And they remember who had the idea.
screen: `SALMAN THE PERSIAN.` · `A STONE AGAINST THE HUNGER.` · `HEARTS ROSE INTO THROATS.` · `A WIND, AND THEY LEFT.` · then, large: `DIG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a good idea from an outsider. Sit, and think of a problem you've been stuck on. Now think of who you haven't asked. The new person at work. Someone from a different country or generation. A kid. Someone whose way of doing things is nothing like yours. Imagine asking them, and actually listening, the way the Prophet listened to Salman. Then picture everyone digging together. The bell holds the time.
The Trench. Salman the Persian's idea, dug by the Muslims of Medina, the Prophet among them, that held back an army of ten thousand. Today's word.
Your line: dig together. Today, ask one outsider for their idea, and do the work alongside the people you're with. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

269.title: Aisha's necklace
269.hook: a lost necklace, a vicious rumor, and verses clearing Aisha (24:11–20)
269.howItsDone: Muslim teachers use the story of the ifk, the slander, and 24:11–20 as the Qur'an's core teaching against spreading unverified accusations and gossip.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trench, a Persian's idea dug by a whole city. Your line was dig together. Did you ask an outsider, and listen? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

A rumor starts as one sentence from one person. Then it's in three group chats. By evening, people who've never met the person involved are sure about what happened, and nobody can quite say who said it first. In Medina, a rumor like that fastened onto Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she told the story herself, in a long account kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. It started with something tiny. On the way home from a journey, in the dark, she realized her necklace was gone. Today: Aisha's necklace.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE, THREE GROUP CHATS.` → `ABOUT THE PROPHET'S WIFE.` → `A NECKLACE, LOST IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Aisha went back to look for her necklace. While she was gone, the men who carried her curtained litter lifted it onto the camel, thinking she was inside. She was young and light, she said, and they didn't notice. The army left. She came back to an empty camp, sat down, and fell asleep. A companion named Safwan, riding behind the army, found her in the morning, let her ride his camel, and walked it by the reins until they caught up. That was all. But some people in Medina saw them arrive together, and a few began to talk. The story grew. Aisha got sick and didn't even know what was being said about her for weeks. When she found out, she said she cried for two nights without sleeping. The Prophet waited, and no revelation came for a month. Finally she said she could only say what Jacob said when his sons came with their lie about Joseph: patience is beautiful, and God is the one to ask for help. Then the verses came, in Surah an-Nur. They cleared her. And they turned on the rumor itself. Why, when you heard it, didn't you think well of your own people and say, this is an obvious lie? You passed it from tongue to tongue, and took it lightly, and to God it was enormous. Sunni Muslims read these verses as clearing Aisha. Some Shia commentators connect them to a different accusation, against another of the Prophet's household. Both read in them the same command: don't carry it.
screen: `A LITTER LIFTED, EMPTY.` · `A MONTH OF SILENCE.` · `PATIENCE IS BEAUTIFUL.` · `FROM TONGUE TO TONGUE.` · then, large: `DON'T CARRY THE RUMOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse to pass on a rumor. Sit, and think of something you've heard about someone lately that you don't actually know is true. A story about a coworker, a relative, a public figure. Notice the little itch to tell it. Now picture it stopping with you. You hear it, and it goes nowhere. Imagine what you'd say instead, close to the verse's own words: it's not for us to speak of this. If you pray, you can ask God to guard your tongue. The bell holds the time.
Aisha's necklace. The small loss that set off a cruel rumor, and the verses in Surah an-Nur that answered it. Today's word.
Your line: don't carry the rumor. Today, when a story about someone reaches you, let it stop with you. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

270.title: Home life
270.hook: he mended his own sandals, patched his clothes, and helped at home (Bukhari)
270.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often hold up the Prophet's home life as a model for husbands and fathers sharing housework, often quoting Aisha's answer and the hadith that the best of you are the best to their families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha's necklace, and a rumor that should have stopped. Your line was don't carry the rumor. Did a story reach you, and stop there? Day two hundred seventy.

For days now we've been with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in big moments: battles, treaties, sieges, revelations. It's easy to imagine a man who only ever stood in front of crowds. So somebody once asked Aisha the most ordinary question you could ask about him. What did he do at home? Not in the mosque. Not on the battlefield. At home, with the door shut, when nobody important was watching. It's a good question to ask about anyone. People can be quite different in their own kitchens. Her answer is short, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it. Today: home life.
screen: `BATTLES, TREATIES, CROWDS.` → `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `AISHA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha says: he used to be busy serving his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. Serving his family. The leader of a whole community, at home, helping. Other reports fill in the picture. Asked again, she said he mended his own sandals, patched his own clothes, milked his goat, and did the kinds of work that men do in their homes. He served himself. He didn't wait for someone to fix things for him. And home itself was simple. His rooms were small, built against the wall of the mosque, with ceilings low enough to touch. His bed, Bukhari says, was leather stuffed with palm fiber. Once Umar came in and saw the marks the rough mat had pressed into the Prophet's side, and he wept, thinking of the emperors of Persia and Rome in their luxury. The Prophet answered him gently: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the next? Aisha also remembered months when no fire was lit in their houses for cooking: they lived on dates and water. None of this was a show. It was just how he lived. And he put it into words in a hadith in at-Tirmidhi: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. Teachers often draw a quiet standard from it: whatever someone is in public, the measure is taken at home, with the sandals and the patches and the dishes.
screen: `BUSY SERVING HIS FAMILY.` · `SANDALS, PATCHES, THE GOAT.` · `A MAT THAT MARKED HIS SIDE.` · `THE BEST TO THEIR FAMILIES.` · then, large: `HE MENDED HIS OWN SHOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one chore you usually skip. Sit, and picture your home. What's the task you always leave for someone else, or for later? The shoes by the door. The button that fell off. The dishes someone else usually does. The trash nobody wants to take out. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it, carefully, as if it matters, because in this story it does. If you live alone, pick the one you avoid the most. The bell holds the time.
Home life. The Prophet at home: serving his family, mending his own sandals and clothes, and living simply. Today's word.
Your line: he mended his own shoes. Today, do that one skipped chore, and don't announce it. Day two hundred seventy.

271.title: The children
271.hook: he let his grandsons Hasan and Husayn climb on him during prayer
271.howItsDone: Children are commonly brought to mosques, and many Muslims cite these hadith to argue for welcoming them, tolerating their noise, and treating them with gentleness and affection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, home life, the Prophet serving his family. Your line was he mended his own shoes. Which skipped chore did you do? Day two hundred seventy-one.

The mosque in Medina is full. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is leading the prayer, and the whole congregation goes down into prostration behind him, foreheads to the ground. And they stay down. And stay down. It's taking far too long. People start wondering: has something happened? Has revelation come? Is he all right? One man lifts his head to look. And there, on the Prophet's back, sitting like he's riding a camel, is a small boy, his grandson, very pleased with himself. The Prophet isn't getting up until the boy is ready to climb off. Today: the children.
screen: `THE WHOLE MOSQUE BOWS DOWN.` → `AND STAYS DOWN.` → `A BOY ON HIS BACK.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i. After the prayer, people told him: you made the prostration so long we thought something had happened. And he said: none of that happened. My son was riding on me, and I didn't want to rush him until he'd had enough. The boy was Hasan or Husayn, the sons of his daughter Fatimah. He called his grandsons his sons. And it wasn't a one-off. Sahih al-Bukhari says he sometimes prayed carrying his granddaughter Umamah: he'd put her down when he bowed and pick her up again when he stood. He said he'd sometimes start a prayer meaning to make it long, hear a baby crying in the back, and shorten it, because he knew how the mother felt. Once, a man named al-Aqra' saw him kissing Hasan and said, I have ten children and I've never kissed a single one of them. The Prophet looked at him and said: whoever doesn't show mercy won't be shown mercy. And he noticed children's small worlds. A little boy named Abu 'Umayr had a pet bird that died, and every time the Prophet saw him, he'd ask, in a rhyme, O Abu 'Umayr, what happened to the little bird? And Anas, who worked in his house from the age of about ten, said: I served him for ten years, and he never once said to me, ugh, and never asked why I did something or why I didn't. Muslims often read these as small stories. They aren't. A prophet in prayer, the most serious moment of his day, waited for a child.
screen: `MY SON WAS RIDING ON ME.` · `UMAMAH IN HIS ARMS.` · `A BABY CRIES, THE PRAYER IS SHORT.` · `NEVER ONCE SAID UGH.` · then, large: `THE CHILD ON HIS BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with a child. Sit, and think of a child in your life: your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or the child you once were. Picture a moment when they slow you down. The endless why. The shoe that won't go on. The story that takes forever. Now picture yourself staying down, like the Prophet in prostration, until they're done. No rushing. The bell holds the time.
The children. How the Prophet was with them: a grandson on his back in prayer, a granddaughter in his arms, a question about a little bird. Today's word.
Your line: the child on his back. Today, when a child slows you down, let them, just once, all the way. Day two hundred seventy-one.

272.title: The animals
272.hook: he told of a sinner forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (Bukhari)
272.howItsDone: Some Muslims leave water out for birds and stray animals in hot weather, citing the hadith of the thirsty dog, and Islamic legal works set out duties of care toward working and domestic animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the children, and a prayer that waited for a boy. Your line was the child on his back. Did a child slow you down, and did you let them? Day two hundred seventy-two.

A man is walking a desert road on a brutally hot day, and he's desperate for water. He finds a well, climbs down into it, drinks, and climbs back up. And there, at the top, is a dog. Panting, tongue out, so thirsty it's licking the damp mud around the well. The man thinks: this dog is feeling exactly what I was feeling a minute ago. He has no bucket. He has no cup. What would you do? Walk on? It's a dog, and you've had your drink. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told this story to his companions, and the ending surprised them so much they had to ask him a question. Today: the animals.
screen: `A DESERT ROAD, A WELL.` → `A DOG LICKING THE MUD.` → `NO BUCKET, NO CUP.`

segments.voice: The man climbed back down the well. He filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth so he could use both hands to climb, came up, and gave the dog a drink. And the Prophet said, in the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: God thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions asked: messenger of God, is there really a reward for us in animals? And he answered with a line Muslims still quote: in every living creature there is reward. Another version of the story, also in Bukhari, makes it even sharper: the one who gave the water was a woman known for sin, and she was forgiven for it. And the Prophet told the other side too. A woman locked up a cat, didn't feed it, and didn't let it go to find food, until it died, and he said she was punished for it. The same care shows up in the stories of his own life. Companions on a journey once took two chicks from a bird's nest, and the mother bird circled over them in distress. The Prophet asked, who has troubled this bird by taking her young? Give them back to her. And one day in a garden in Medina a camel saw him and moaned, with tears in its eyes. He went to it, stroked it until it calmed, then found its owner and told him: don't you fear God concerning this animal? It has told me you starve it and wear it out. The Qur'an says that every creature on earth and every bird on two wings are communities, like you.
screen: `WATER IN HIS LEATHER SOCK.` · `IN EVERY LIVING CREATURE, REWARD.` · `GIVE THE BIRD HER YOUNG.` · `COMMUNITIES, LIKE YOU.` · then, large: `WATER FOR THE DOG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put out water for an animal. If you can, do it now, or plan it: a bowl on the step, a dish in the yard, fresh water for a pet whose bowl you haven't checked. Then sit, and think about the animals near you that you mostly don't notice. Birds on the wire. A neighbor's dog. The cat in the alley. Picture each one, for a moment, as a community of its own. The bell holds the time.
The animals. The Prophet's teaching that there's reward in every living creature, from a thirsty dog to a grieving bird. Today's word.
Your line: water for the dog. Today, do one kind thing for an animal, even a small one, and remember it counts. Day two hundred seventy-two.

273.title: The treaty at Hudaybiyyah
273.hook: they come as pilgrims, are turned back, and sign a treaty that looks like a loss
273.howItsDone: Muslims study Hudaybiyyah as a model of patient diplomacy and of accepting hard terms for peace, and the story of Umm Salamah's advice is often told as an example of wise counsel from the Prophet's wives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the animals, and a dog given water from a leather sock. Your line was water for the dog. Did you do one kind thing for an animal? Day two hundred seventy-three, the end of a week.

Years after leaving Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has a dream that he and his companions enter the Sacred Mosque in peace. So he sets out, with about fourteen hundred people. Not as an army. As pilgrims, dressed in the simple cloth of pilgrimage, driving animals to sacrifice, carrying only travelers' swords in their sheaths. They want to do the 'umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, and go home. But the Meccans block the road. At a place called al-Hudaybiyyah, just outside the sacred boundary, the pilgrims stop. Messengers go back and forth. Tension builds. And in the end, there's a treaty, and on the Muslim side, the companions can hardly bear it. Today: the treaty at Hudaybiyyah.
screen: `A DREAM OF THE SACRED MOSQUE.` → `FOURTEEN HUNDRED PILGRIMS.` → `THE ROAD IS BLOCKED.`

segments.voice: Mecca's negotiator was Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and the story of the writing is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet told 'Ali to write: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Suhayl objected: we don't know this Merciful. Write, in your name, O God, the old way. The Prophet agreed. Then: this is what Muhammad, the messenger of God, has agreed. Suhayl objected again: if we believed you were God's messenger, we wouldn't be fighting you. Write Muhammad son of 'Abdullah. 'Ali couldn't bring himself to erase it. So the Prophet asked him to point to the words, and erased them with his own hand. Then the terms. The Muslims go home this year, no pilgrimage. They can come back next year, for three days. And, the biographers add, ten years of peace. And if anyone from Mecca runs to the Muslims, they must be sent back, but not the other way around. Right then, a young Muslim named Abu Jandal, Suhayl's own son, stumbled into the camp in chains, begging to be taken in. And he was sent back. The companions were shattered. Umar went to the Prophet and asked: aren't we in the right? The Prophet said: I am God's messenger, and I won't disobey him. Then he told the people to sacrifice their animals and shave their heads, ending the pilgrimage where they stood, and nobody moved. He went into the tent of his wife Umm Salamah, hurt. She told him: go out, say nothing to anyone, sacrifice your animal and call for your barber. He did. And when they saw him do it, they all rose and did the same.
screen: `IN YOUR NAME, O GOD.` · `HE ERASED IT HIMSELF.` · `ABU JANDAL, SENT BACK.` · `UMM SALAMAH'S ADVICE.` · then, large: `IT LOOKED LIKE LOSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a hard compromise. Sit, and think of something you're fighting over right now. A plan at work, a family decision, an argument with a partner. Ask honestly: what would I give up to make peace here? Not what's right, what's wise. The word you'd erase. The title you'd let go of. Picture yourself doing it with your own hand, without a speech. Then look back at this week: Hamzah, the Trench, the necklace, home, children, animals, and now a treaty that hurt. The bell holds the time.
The treaty at Hudaybiyyah. The peace signed outside Mecca in which the Muslims gave up the pilgrimage, the title and even a refugee, and which looked like a loss. Today's word.
Your line: it looked like losing. Today, let one small thing go for the sake of peace, and see what grows in the space it leaves. Day two hundred seventy-three.
